summary: A republication of RFC 1944 that corrects the IP addresses assigned as defaults for network test equipment. It describes methods for benchmarking network interconnect devices such as routers. It obsoletes RFC 1944 and was updated by RFC 6201, RFC 6815 and RFC 9004.

eli5.summary: This is a rulebook for fairly testing how fast network boxes are, so every test is done the same way. This version fixes the addresses used in testing.

questions: what is a device under test
subtitle: A fixed recipe for testing routers and bridges so vendors' speed claims can be compared fairly.

tldr.problem: Vendors of network devices often engage in specsmanship, so buyers cannot compare one product's performance claims with another's.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a common test setup, frame sizes, traffic conditions and six benchmark tests (throughput, latency, frame loss rate, back-to-back frames, system recovery and reset), plus how to report each result.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. It replaces RFC 1944 (a republication with corrected test IP addresses) and has been updated by RFC 6201, RFC 6815 and RFC 9004.

today: RFC 2544 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1944, and it has been updated by RFC 6201, RFC 6815 and RFC 9004. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why a Standard Benchmark Suite
sections.content:
The RFC opens by naming the problem: vendors often engage in specsmanship to give their products a better position in the marketplace, sometimes with "smoke and mirrors" that confuse buyers. It defines one set of tests that vendors can run and report, so users get comparable data from different vendors.

The terms it uses (such as throughput and latency) come from RFC 1242, which the reader is told to consult first. The authors admit they know of no off-the-shelf equipment that implements every test, but believe such equipment can be built. Not every test applies to every device, and vendors should run the ones their product supports.

The RFC also warns that the results need judgment. A router's rate for IPX frames matters little to a site that does not use IPX, and the tests should be read with repeatability, variance and statistical significance in mind.
sections.eli5: Companies like to brag about how fast their gear is, but each one measures differently. This RFC says: everybody take the same test, then the numbers can be compared.

sections.title: Test Setup, Frames and Device Configuration
sections.content:
The ideal setup is a tester with both sending and receiving ports. It sends traffic into the device under test (DUT) and receives it back, so it can tell whether every frame came through and whether the right frames arrived. Separate sender and receiver machines work too, but the labor can be prohibitive unless they are controlled as one tester. For a DUT that joins different media, such as Ethernet and FDDI, either a tester with both media or two identical DUTs back to back can be used.

The DUT MUST be configured as the vendor instructs, with all supported protocols enabled, and the configuration must not be tuned between tests. For example, it is not acceptable to change frame buffer sizes between tests or to disable all but one protocol. The software version and exact configuration MUST be included in the report.

Every test SHOULD be run at several frame sizes, at least five. For Ethernet the recommended sizes are 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280, 1518. For 4Mb and 16Mb token ring and for FDDI they are 54, 64, 128, 256, 1024, 1518, 2048, 4472. The unrealistically small sizes are there to show the per-frame processing overhead of the DUT.

The tester should discard anything that is not a forwarded test frame (keep-alives and routing updates, for example) and check frame lengths. Ideally it puts sequence numbers in the frames so it can report frames dropped, out of order, duplicated and gaps in the numbering.
sections.eli5: You put a box in the middle, a tester on both sides, and send the same kinds of packages every time. You are not allowed to tweak the box to do better on one test.

sections.title: Modifiers and Traffic Conditions
sections.content:
The suite SHOULD first be run with a plain stream of frames, then repeated under each modifier separately. Modifier frames replace one of the normal test frames in the same stream rather than arriving on another port.

  • Broadcast frames: 1% of the stream, for example every 100th frame, is addressed to the hardware broadcast address. The RFC says this is much higher than many networks see, but a high level is needed to see an effect that would otherwise hide in normal variation.
  • Management frames: one management query (such as SNMP) as the first frame of each second.
  • Routing updates: routing update frames that alternate between two states, A and B, which MUST be alternated during the trial.
  • Filters: first one filter that permits the test stream, then 25 filters, where the first 24 block other addresses and the last one permits the test stream, so 25 conditions are checked before a frame matches.

Other conditions covered include random destination addresses spread over 256 networks, bidirectional traffic, multi-port devices where half the ports are inputs and half are outputs, and bursty traffic with burst sizes of 16, 64, 256 and 1024 frames. FDDI devices SHOULD be tested with 1, 4, 8 and 16 frames per token.
sections.eli5: After the plain test, you make things harder on purpose: some shouting to everyone, some questions, some changed maps and a long list of rules to check. Then you see whether the box slows down.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Trial
sections.content:
A test is made of many trials, each producing one piece of information, such as the loss rate at one input rate. A trial has fixed phases:

  1. If the DUT is a router, send the routing update and pause two seconds.
  2. Send the learning frames to the output port and wait two seconds. Learning frames prime the bridge tables or address resolution tables of the DUT.
  3. Run the test trial.
  4. Wait two seconds for residual frames.
  5. Wait at least five seconds for the DUT to restabilize.

The test portion of each trial SHOULD last at least 60 seconds, because the aim is the rate the DUT can support continuously. Tests that use a binary search, such as the throughput test, may use shorter trials while searching, but the final result SHOULD come from full-length trials.

Before each trial a routing update MUST be sent that carries every network address the trial needs, all resolving to the same next hop. For LAN tests the frame rate SHOULD be the listed theoretical maximum for the frame size. For WAN tests it SHOULD be higher, to allow for header compression.
sections.eli5: Every run follows the same routine: get ready, wait a moment, run, wait for stragglers, and rest. That way each run starts from the same place.

sections.title: The Six Benchmark Tests
sections.content:
Section 26 defines the tests, each with an objective, a procedure and a reporting format.

  • Throughput: send a known number of frames at a rate and count what comes out. If any are lost, lower the rate and rerun. Throughput is the fastest rate at which the received count equals the sent count. A single advertised figure MUST be in frames per second and state the measured rate, the frame size, the media's theoretical limit and the protocol.
  • Latency: at the throughput rate, send a stream of at least 120 seconds with a tagged frame after 60 seconds, and subtract the send timestamp from the receive timestamp. Repeat at least 20 times and report the average.
  • Frame loss rate: compute ((input_count - output_count) * 100) / input_count. Start at 100% of the maximum rate and step down by 10% (finer is encouraged) until two successive trials lose nothing.
  • Back-to-back frames: find the longest burst with minimum gaps that is forwarded with no loss. Trials last at least 2 seconds and SHOULD be repeated at least 50 times.
  • System recovery: overload at 110% of throughput (or the media maximum, whichever is lower) for at least 60 seconds, drop to 50%, and time when the last loss occurs.
  • Reset: send frames at the throughput rate for the minimum frame size, cause a reset and time how long forwarding takes to resume. A power interruption test cuts power for 10 seconds.
sections.eli5: There are six checks: how fast it can go without dropping anything, how long a package takes to cross, how many get lost when pushed too hard, how big a rush it can take, how fast it recovers from being swamped, and how fast it wakes up after a restart.

sections.title: Appendices: Rates, Addresses and Test Frames
sections.content:
The appendices give reference material. Appendix B lists the maximum frame rates in frames per second. For 64-byte frames that is 14880 on Ethernet, 24691 on 16Mb token ring and 152439 on FDDI. For 1518-byte frames it is 812, 1302 and 8138.

Appendix C defines example frames for TCP/IP over Ethernet. The test frame is a UDP Echo Request, chosen because a datagram protocol avoids session setup that a router might expect and because some routers refuse to forward unknown protocols. Data in the frame should not be all zero bits or all ones, since that can trigger bit stuffing on WAN links. Input ports use Class C networks from 198.18.1.0 to 198.18.64.0 and output ports use 198.19.1.0 to 198.19.64.0, with the router at node 1. The IESG note explains that this RFC exists to correct the test IP addresses of RFC 1944.

Routing update intervals are listed as 30 seconds for IP RIP and 90 seconds for IGRP and OSPF. The RFC also states that security issues are not addressed in the document.
sections.eli5: The back of the rulebook has the reference tables and a sample package to copy, plus the special addresses reserved for testing so nobody mixes up test traffic with real traffic.
